analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals to meet minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios and protects nurses who refuse or report unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees for 20 months without ever getting a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended, despite 57 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced every US hospital — including VA, military, and Indian Health Service hospitals — to keep a minimum number of registered nurses on each shift, with specific patient limits by unit type: one nurse per patient in operating and trauma units, up to one nurse per four patients in medical/surgical units. Hospitals would have to post their actual staffing in public view, keep records open to nurses and the public, and submit to federal audits. Nurses could refuse assignments that broke the limits or that they were not trained for, and hospitals could not fire or punish them for refusing or for reporting violations. Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted to cover the extra cost. The bill was introduced in May 2007 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be cared for under guaranteed minimum staffing levels; the bill's findings cite studies linking higher registered-nurse staffing to lower rates of patient injury and death. Registered nurses also benefit directly: caps on how many patients each nurse can be assigned, the right to refuse unsafe assignments without losing their license, and federal protection against being fired or reported to state licensing boards for refusing or reporting violations. Rural hospitals get up to four years to come into compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Sets hard maximum patient loads per nurse by unit type — one patient in operating and trauma units, two in intensive care, three in emergency rooms, four in medical/surgical units — with federal audits to check compliance [S2][S3].

Gives nurses the right to refuse assignments that would violate staffing limits or that they are not trained for, and bans hospitals from firing or retaliating against nurses who refuse or report violations, with the right to sue for reinstatement and lost wages [S2][S3].
Requires hospitals to post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit where staff, patients, and the public can see them, and to keep staffing records open to nurses and the public [S3].

Bases the bill's findings on studies linking understaffing to patient harm, including a 2002 Joint Commission report attributing nearly a quarter of unanticipated patient deaths and injuries to a lack of direct-care registered nurses [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire significantly more registered nurses to meet the ratios — the bill acknowledges this by requiring the Secretary to adjust Medicare payments to cover the net additional costs hospitals incur, meaning federal taxpayers would also absorb part of the bill. Hospitals in rural areas and those already operating on thin margins would face the steepest compliance burden, and the bill authorizes federal appropriations for VA, military, and other federally operated hospitals to comply.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would be expensive, and the burden would fall hardest on rural and financially struggling hospitals: the bill gives rural hospitals up to four years to comply with the ratios, an acknowledgment that smaller facilities would have trouble meeting them sooner [S3].
The bill cannot create the nurses it requires. Hospitals can only meet the ratios by hiring, and during a nurse shortage some hospitals might close beds or cut other services to comply [S3].

Fixed numeric ratios are a blunt instrument compared with staffing plans calibrated to patient acuity; the bill requires ratios above the minimum where acuity demands, but critics of ratio mandates argue rigid numbers can misallocate nurses across units [S3].

Taxpayers would absorb part of the cost: the bill directs the Secretary to adjust Medicare payments to hospitals to cover net additional compliance costs, shifting a share of the mandate onto the federal budget [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: the record in the bill cites evidence linking understaffing to avoidable patient deaths, and the bill would give nurses real protection to refuse and report unsafe assignments. The costs are also real and unevenly spread: hospitals would bear the immediate expense of hiring more nurses, rural and financially struggling hospitals would have the hardest time complying, and because Medicare reimbursement would be adjusted upward, part of the bill would land on taxpayers. A legitimate design question is whether fixed national ratios are too rigid compared with flexible acuity-based staffing plans, and whether a federal mandate is the best way to address a nursing shortage the mandate itself cannot create nurses to fill. The bigger issue for this analysis is that none of that debate ever happened: the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced May 3, 2007 by Rep. Jan Schakowsky with 56 cosponsors, 54 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S1][S4][S5].
Referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S5].
The record shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — for the remaining 20 months of the 110th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and their owners came out ahead: they avoided the recurring cost of hiring enough nurses to meet fixed ratios, and no staffing limits or whistleblower protections took effect. Patients and nurses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, which avoided the staffing costs

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in May 2007 and recruited nine original cosponsors including two committee chairmen.

for.name: 54 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill during the 110th Congress.

for.name: Nursing unions and nurse associations
for.what_they_did: Long advocated for mandatory nurse-to-patient ratios and backed this approach; they had no recorded action in the bill's history.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in May 2007, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup in the remaining 20 months of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY), an original cosponsor of the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by sequential referral and took no recorded action on it during the Congress.

against.name: American Hospital Association and the hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federally mandated nurse-to-patient ratios as an inflexible staffing mandate; the industry had no recorded role in this bill's fate.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 54 of 233 House Democrats versus 2 of 202 House Republicans — though the bill died in committees chaired by members of the majority party, not on a floor vote.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to hire significantly more registered nurses to meet fixed ratios, a major recurring labor cost, with a Medicare payment adjustment covering only part of it. The industry would bear the compliance burden of a federal mandate on its largest controllable expense.

Nurses would gain legal caps on patient loads, the right to refuse unsafe assignments, and protection from retaliation for reporting staffing violations — protections aimed at retention of nurses who leave bedside care over workload.

Hospitals filling mandated ratios during a shortage would likely lean harder on agency and temporary nurses, whose higher rates the bill's costs would flow through; the bill's requirements apply to these nurses as well.
